question: Can a lightweight fixed-point module canonicalize spatially varying scale transformations inside pretrained vision backbones, improving local-scale consistency without rebuilding the backbone as an equivariant architecture?

key_findings.claim: The paper replaces physically general local rescaling with an invertible monotone-warp group so that canonicalization can be formulated with group actions.
key_findings.evidence: In one dimension, continuous strictly increasing bijections of the unit interval form a group under composition. The image construction uses piecewise-linear two-dimensional coordinate warps and restricts local Jacobians to be symmetric positive definite and mutually commuting, which the appendix uses to argue closure and inverse existence.

anchors.section: A2.2 Two-Dimensional Monotone Scaling Group, Lemma 2

key_findings.claim: DEC amortizes per-example canonicalization as a learned equilibrium state and inserts inverse/forward warps around multiple latent modules.
key_findings.evidence: A two-layer convolutional update predicts monotone-warp parameters, Anderson acceleration iterates it to a fixed point, and implicit differentiation trains through that point. Each adapted module first inversely warps its input feature and, for equivariant tasks, re-applies the warp to its output; invariant tasks omit the output warp. Repeating this construction at multiple modules outperforms input-only canonicalization in the MNIST ablation.

anchors.section: A5.2 Additional Ablation Study, Table A3

key_findings.claim: On synthetic local-scale segmentation, DEC gives consistent but modest gains over augmentation and an equivariance-loss baseline.
key_findings.evidence: Across ViT, Swin, and DINOv2 on 6,000 training and 2,000 test renderings, DEC has the highest mIoU and lowest equivariance error in every column. Relative to the strongest baseline per architecture, mIoU gains are 0.77, 0.93, and 1.81 points, while equivariance-error reductions are 0.002, 0.001, and 0.003.

key_findings.claim: Local-scale MNIST shows the largest and most replicated improvements.
key_findings.evidence: On 1,000-way classification of three independently resized digits with 6,000 training and 50,000 test images, DEC is best across ResNet, ViT, DeiT, Swin, BEiT, and DINOv2. Averaged across the six architectures, the paper reports a 4.10-point accuracy gain over augmentation and an invariance-error reduction of 8.91 times 10^-2; Table 2 gives five-run error bars. For Swin, accuracy remains higher in all tested scale brackets, including the extrapolative [2,3] range.

key_findings.claim: ImageNet gains are broad but small and are measured on a synthetic object-editing pipeline rather than naturally observed local scale changes.
key_findings.evidence: Target objects are detected with Grounding DINO, segmented with SAM, removed with LaMa inpainting, resized within [0.7,1.3], and pasted back. After fine-tuning on 10,000 such images and testing on 50,000, DEC improves top-1 accuracy over the base by 0.21 to 0.38 points across ViT, DeiT, Swin, and BEiT while slightly reducing invariance error; the table does not report run-to-run uncertainty for these comparisons.

key_findings.claim: The paper does not establish the exact equivariance guarantee suggested by the canonicalization equations for the learned DEC implementation.
key_findings.evidence: Claim 1 only shows that a fixed point of the specifically defined gradient update has zero energy gradient, and then incorrectly labels any stationary point a local minimum. Immediately afterward, the implemented method replaces that gradient update with an unconstrained learned neural update. No proof shows that its fixed point minimizes an energy, that its predicted canonicalizer satisfies h(T(f,g)) = g h(f), or that finite Anderson iterations preserve that relation. The empirical errors are nonzero, so the supported result is improved consistency, not exact equivariance.

anchors.section: Claim 1, Equations 16–19, and learned update replacement

key_findings.claim: The two-dimensional parameterization is not proven to realize the exact transformation group used in the theory.
key_findings.evidence: The abstract group requires symmetric-positive-definite, pairwise-commuting Jacobians, but the implemented warp is built by independently monotone row and column functions plus bilinear interpolation. The text does not prove that this construction has symmetric positive-definite or mutually commuting Jacobians, and its inverse is approximated by separately inverting row/column functions rather than solving the coupled two-dimensional inverse. Therefore the exact group-action assumptions need not hold for the sampled transformations.

method.core_idea: Define an invertible monotone spatial-warp surrogate for local object scaling, predict a canonical warp through a deep-equilibrium fixed point, and wrap successive pretrained latent modules with inverse and forward feature warps.
method.mechanism: A lightweight convolutional map iteratively updates a grid of monotone-warp parameters until an Anderson-accelerated equilibrium. Latent features are resampled into the predicted canonical frame before a backbone block; equivariant outputs are then resampled back, while invariant classification retains the canonical frame.
assumptions: Real local object-scale changes can be usefully approximated by smooth invertible monotone coordinate warps, excluding occlusion, disocclusion, and topology changes.
The discretized two-dimensional warp and its numerical inverse behave like elements of the theoretical monotone transformation group.
A learned fixed point acts as a consistent canonical choice even though the implemented update is not constrained to be energy descent or an equivariant canonicalizer.
Synthetic object cutout, inpainting, and paste operations provide a faithful test of real-world local-scale robustness.
Feature-map resampling across heterogeneous pretrained modules retains a meaningful common spatial action.

techniques.role: Replaces noninvertible physical local scaling with an invertible transformation family amenable to group-based canonicalization.
Amortizes per-example canonical parameter search as a constant-memory implicit fixed-point layer.
Adapts pretrained backbones at multiple intermediate features instead of distorting only the input image.
Measures squared prediction disagreement under known monotone warps for segmentation and classification.
Creates controlled object-wise scale interventions for segmentation, multi-digit recognition, and ImageNet classification.

evaluations.setting: Synthetic Google Scanned Objects segmentation with two independently scaled objects, 6,000 training and 2,000 test images
evaluations.metric: Mean intersection-over-union and monotone-scale equivariance error
evaluations.result: DEC is best across ViT, Swin, and DINOv2, improving mIoU over the strongest baseline by 0.77 to 1.81 points and reducing error by 0.001 to 0.003.
evaluations.baseline: Monotone-warp augmentation, input-only canonicalization, and augmentation plus equivariance loss.

evaluations.setting: Locally scaled three-digit MNIST with 6,000 training and 50,000 test images over 1,000 classes
evaluations.metric: Top-1 accuracy and invariance error over five runs
evaluations.result: DEC is best for all six backbones and reportedly improves average accuracy over augmentation by 4.10 points while lowering average invariance error by 0.0891.
evaluations.baseline: Augmentation, input canonicalization, and augmentation plus invariance loss across ResNet, ViT, DeiT, Swin, BEiT, and DINOv2.

evaluations.setting: Locally edited ImageNet with one detected object resized in [0.7,1.3], 10,000 fine-tuning and 50,000 evaluation images
evaluations.metric: Top-1 accuracy, invariance error, and accuracy at seven scale factors
evaluations.result: DEC improves base accuracy by 0.21 to 0.38 points across four transformer backbones, slightly reduces invariance error, and is best at every reported Swin scale.
evaluations.baseline: Pretrained-model fine-tuning, scale augmentation, input canonicalization, and invariance-loss fine-tuning.

evaluations.setting: Memory and runtime comparison at batch size 10 with 224-by-224 inputs
evaluations.metric: GPU memory and seconds per iteration
evaluations.result: DEC uses 5.75 GB and 0.19 seconds versus 43.30 GB and 0.41 seconds for differentiable optimization-based canonicalization.
The DEC module takes 0.16 seconds of a 0.66-second total, or 24% overhead.
evaluations.baseline: Backbone-plus-remaining computation time without the DEC module.

limitations: Author-stated: monotone scaling is only an approximation to physical local scale changes, which may be noninvertible because of occlusion.
Author-stated: why the learned canonical warp benefits a backbone remains difficult to interpret, and group-element interpretability is underexplored.
Reviewer-identified: the learned fixed-point map lacks the canonicalizer-equivariance constraint required for an exact mathematical guarantee.
Reviewer-identified: the stationary-point argument neither proves a local minimum nor applies after the gradient update is replaced by an unconstrained neural update.
Reviewer-identified: the implemented two-dimensional interpolation/inversion is not shown to satisfy the symmetric-positive-definite and commutative-Jacobian group restrictions.
Reviewer-identified: ImageNet gains are small, lack uncertainty in the main table, and use detector/segmenter/inpainting artifacts that may be correlated with the method's resampling operations.
Reviewer-identified: comparison omits stronger continuous-group canonicalization methods and scale-equivariant architectures on the same local-scale protocol.
Reviewer-identified: DEC adds iterative inference, with a reported 24% share of DINOv2 processing time in one setup.
failure_modes: The fixed-point solver can converge to different or unstable equilibria without producing a transformation-consistent canonical frame.
Latent resampling may blur small objects or alias high-frequency features, especially under extreme or non-monotone physical deformations.
Cutout-and-inpainting artifacts can make the synthetic local-scale benchmark measure editing-pipeline robustness rather than natural perspective or object-size robustness.
Independent coordinate-wise inverse approximations can deviate from the inverse of a coupled two-dimensional warp.
Repeated canonicalization can improve accuracy through extra trainable capacity rather than the claimed symmetry mechanism unless matched-capacity controls are included.
reusable_insights: When a nuisance transformation is not a group, explicitly separate the physically realistic operation from the invertible surrogate used for theory.
Latent canonicalization can preserve the input distribution better than warping raw inputs, but it needs matched-capacity and action-consistency controls.
An implicit layer is a useful amortizer for per-example optimization only if its fixed-point constraints preserve the properties of the original optimization problem.
Evaluate symmetry methods jointly on task accuracy, transformation consistency, inference cost, and unmodified inputs.
Synthetic transformation benchmarks should include artifact controls and naturally captured test sets.
open_questions: Can the DEC update be parameterized so its fixed point provably satisfies the canonicalizer relation for the implemented finite-dimensional warp family?
Does the two-dimensional interpolation actually define a globally invertible group action, and can its inverse be computed exactly and differentiably?
How much of the gain remains against a parameter- and compute-matched latent resampling module without canonicalization semantics?
Do improvements transfer to naturally captured multi-object scale changes with occlusion and depth variation?
Can adaptive or Lie-algebra canonicalization handle the same local-warp family with stronger continuity or equivariance guarantees?
What accuracy-consistency-cost Pareto frontier results from varying equilibrium tolerance and the number of adapted latent modules?

competitive_landscape.title: Scale-Equivariant Steerable Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Sosnovik, Szmaja, and Smeulders build exact global scale equivariance into convolution and other blocks with steerable filters. DEC instead adapts arbitrary pretrained backbones and targets spatially varying monotone warps, but supplies empirical consistency rather than a demonstrated exact action constraint.

competitive_landscape.title: Scaling-Translation-Equivariant Networks with Decomposed Convolutional Filters
competitive_landscape.difference: ScDCFNet derives necessary and sufficient group convolutions with low-frequency decomposed filters and deformation robustness for global scaling and translation. DEC avoids architectural replacement and permits position-dependent warps, at the cost of iterative resampling and weaker guarantees.

competitive_landscape.title: Equivariance with Learned Canonicalization Functions
competitive_landscape.difference: Kaba et al. formalize learned canonicalizers, universality, and direct equivariance across several groups and tasks. DEC adds an implicit fixed-point amortizer, a local monotone-warp family, and multi-layer latent insertion, but does not prove its learned fixed point satisfies the predecessor's canonicalizer condition.

competitive_landscape.title: Equivariant Adaptation of Large Pretrained Models
competitive_landscape.difference: Mondal et al. adapt large pretrained models with input canonicalization and dataset-dependent priors to prevent canonical orientations from leaving the training distribution, primarily for rotations. DEC moves canonicalization into several latent stages and targets high-dimensional local warps.

competitive_landscape.title: Lie Algebra Canonicalization: Equivariant Neural Operators under Arbitrary Lie Groups
competitive_landscape.difference: LieLAC uses infinitesimal generators and Lie-group descent to canonicalize pretrained models under continuous, including noncompact, groups while addressing theoretical canonicalization issues. DEC learns faster equilibrium updates for a bespoke finite warp parameterization and evaluates local-scale vision rather than PDE symmetries.

competitive_landscape.title: Adaptive Canonicalization with Application to Invariant Anisotropic Geometric Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Lin and Levie make the canonical choice depend on both input and predictor, prove continuity and symmetry preservation, and address canonicalization discontinuities through prior maximization. DEC predates it and focuses on fast latent fixed points for local image scaling without a comparable continuity or universality proof.

competitive_landscape.title: Deep Equilibrium Models
competitive_landscape.difference: Bai, Kolter, and Koltun introduce root-solved infinite-depth fixed-point networks and implicit differentiation for sequence models. DEC repurposes that machinery to output transformation parameters, which creates a new need to prove that the learned equilibrium is a valid canonicalizer.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The paper claims the first equivariant treatment of local scaling, a new deep-equilibrium canonicalizer, and an effective latent adaptation method for pretrained vision networks.
novelty_assessment.evidence: Prior scale-equivariant architectures focus on global scaling, and prior learned canonicalizers handle lower-dimensional groups or input-level adaptation. DEC combines a position-dependent monotone-warp surrogate, implicit amortized search, and repeated latent canonicalization across six backbones and three controlled benchmarks.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The novel empirical package is credible: an implicit latent warp adapter consistently improves synthetic local-scale accuracy and consistency, especially on low-data multi-digit MNIST. The exact-equivariance novelty is not established because the implemented neural fixed point is not shown to satisfy the canonicalizer law and the finite two-dimensional warp is not shown to realize the theoretical group; current positioning should also acknowledge the later continuity-guaranteed adaptive canonicalization of arXiv:2509.24886.

reviewer_notes: Read all 15 extracted PDF pages, including group definitions and proofs, the fixed-point claim, every main result table, implementation details, runtime, ablations, and learned-warp discussion. Page anchors are PDF pages. Related-work searches covered local/global scale equivariance, learned and pretrained-model canonicalization, continuous-group optimization, fixed-point models, and post-submission canonicalization; seven primary arXiv records were checked through 2026-08-23. The mathematical guarantee concerns are direct audits of the stated equations and appendix construction; code and experiments were not rerun.
